lines.text: Imagine a machine that prints brand-new money.
If a million new dollars came out tomorrow,
would it matter who got them first?
It does. It may be why your rent keeps climbing, and your savings keep shrinking.
It's called the Cantillon Effect.
Three hundred years ago, a Paris banker named Richard Cantillon noticed something.
New money doesn't spread evenly. It enters at one point, and ripples outward.
Picture a tiny town where bread costs one dollar.
New money goes to the banker first. He spends it right away, at yesterday's prices.
Next, it reaches the builder. Prices start to creep up. Then the shopkeeper. Bread hits a dollar fifty.
By the time it reaches the teacher and the retiree, their incomes haven't changed. But bread now costs two dollars.
Nobody stole anything. But wealth quietly moved, from the back of the line to the front.
Today, new money flows first to banks, governments, and big investors,
who buy assets like stocks and real estate before prices move.
Wages are almost always last.
So if you earn a paycheck, your raise shows up after prices have already moved.
If you save in cash, it's like walking up an escalator that's going down.
Meanwhile, people who already own assets get richer, without doing anything differently.
Inflation isn't just prices going up. It's a transfer.
So next time you hear that new money is being created, don't just ask how much.
Ask: who gets it first?
